content: 1. Interventions for managing illness are categorized into four main areas: antenatal care, lifestyle choices, nutrition and diet, and pharmacological interventions. 2. A generic protocol has been developed to guide the creation and maintenance of reviews that evaluate interventions aimed at preventing pre-eclampsia. 3. This protocol provides a standardized methodology for selecting and assessing studies. 4. The protocol was developed in collaboration with existing review authors, whose contributions are acknowledged under the section 'Contributions of reviewers.' 5. The use of this protocol is intended to ensure a systematic and comprehensive approach to the topic, improve consistency across reviews, and make them more accessible and user-friendly. 6. If any review significantly deviates from this protocol, the reasons for such deviations will be explicitly stated. 7. Unlike other protocols in The Cochrane Library, this generic protocol will remain as a protocol and will not be converted into a full review. 8. Reviews developed or updated using this protocol will be published separately in The Cochrane Library. 9. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a common condition during pregnancy. 10. Approximately 10% of pregnant women will have elevated blood pressure recorded at some point before delivery. 11. Pre-eclampsia, also known as toxemia, is defined as hypertension accompanied by proteinuria (protein in the urine). 12. Pre-eclampsia typically occurs in the second half of pregnancy and affects 2% to 8% of pregnancies. 13. For women with hypertension alone, pregnancy outcomes are generally similar to those of women with normal blood pressure. 14. Outcomes worsen when proteinuria develops. 15. Women with mild pre-eclampsia often do not exhibit symptoms. 16. Women with severe pre-eclampsia or very high blood pressure may experience symptoms such as headache, upper abdominal pain, or visual disturbances. 17. Pre-eclampsia can lead to complications involving the liver, kidneys, brain, and clotting system abnormalities. 18. Rare but serious complications include eclampsia (seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia), stroke, HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets), and disseminated intravascular coagulation. 19. These complications are associated with an increased risk of maternal death. 20. The placenta is also affected in pre-eclampsia, increasing risks for the baby. 21. The most common problems for the baby include poor growth and premature birth. 22. While most women recover well after pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, these conditions remain significant causes of maternal mortality. 23. Over half a million women die annually from pregnancy-related causes, with 99% of these deaths occurring in developing countries. 24. An estimated 10% to 15% of maternal deaths in developing countries are linked to pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. 25. In the UK and USA, 13% to 15% of direct obstetric deaths are associated with pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. 26. Perinatal mortality is also higher following pre-eclampsia. 27. There is limited information on morbidity for either the mother or baby, but it is likely to be significant. 28. Pre-eclampsia accounts for approximately one-fifth of antenatal admissions and two-thirds of referrals to day care assessment units in the UK. 29. In France, pre-eclampsia accounts for a quarter of obstetric admissions to intensive care units. 30. For many women, developing pre-eclampsia can be a challenging and unexpected experience, particularly if they become seriously ill, deliver prematurely, or experience the loss of their baby. 31. Psychological morbidity following a difficult pregnancy, labor, or perinatal death is well-documented, although specific data on pre-eclampsia are limited. 32. There is growing evidence that women who have experienced gestational hypertension or pre-eclampsia may have an increased risk later in life of hypertension, stroke, and ischemic heart disease. 33. For babies, pre-eclampsia is a contributing factor in up to 12% of those born small for gestational age and 19% of those born preterm. 34. Such babies are at an increased risk of developmental delays and chronic ill health during childhood. 35. Pre-eclampsia is part of a spectrum of conditions known as hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. 36. These disorders exist on a continuum with normal pregnancy. 37. During normal pregnancy, significant maternal physiological adaptations occur to support the growing fetus and placenta. 38. For example, cardiac output increases by approximately 40% during the first trimester. 39. Blood pressure remains relatively unchanged in the first trimester, decreases by about 5 to 10 mmHg in the second trimester, and returns to pre-pregnancy levels by term. 40. Cardiac output is influenced by peripheral resistance and blood pressure. 41. Normal pregnancy is associated with increased cardiac output and normal or slightly reduced blood pressure, leading to a decrease in peripheral resistance. 42. Changes in kidney function also occur during normal pregnancy, with increased protein excretion, particularly in the third trimester. 43. Protein excretion of up to 300 mg in 24 hours is considered normal during pregnancy. 44. The classification and definitions of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy have historically been controversial. 45. Recently, there has been a shift towards agreeing on standard definitions that are clinically relevant. 46. Hypertension in pregnancy is typically defined as a systolic blood pressure of at least 140 mmHg and/or a diastolic blood pressure of at least 90 mmHg. 47. Any rise in blood pressure should be confirmed by a second measurement, ideally taken at least four hours later. 48. Blood pressure should be measured using an auscultatory device, as oscillometric techniques tend to underestimate blood pressure during pregnancy. 49. The debate over which auscultatory sound to use for diastolic blood pressure assessment—muffling (Korotkoff phase IV) or disappearance (Korotkoff phase V)—has been resolved, with Korotkoff V now recommended as more reliable. 50. The suggestion that changes in blood pressure are more important than absolute levels is no longer included due to a lack of evidence linking it to outcomes. 51. Proteinuria during pregnancy is defined as 300 mg or more of protein in 24 hours. 52. In a single midstream urine sample, this typically corresponds to 30 mg/dL, 1+ or more on a dipstick, or a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio of at least 30 mg/mmol. 53. Four main categories of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are now widely recognized. 54. Gestational hypertension is hypertension detected for the first time during the second half of pregnancy (after 20 weeks of gestation) without proteinuria. 55. Gestational hypertension resolves within three months of birth. 56. Pre-eclampsia is defined as hypertension and proteinuria detected for the first time in the second half of pregnancy (after 20 weeks of gestation). 57. Eclampsia refers to the occurrence of seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia. 58. There is no universally accepted definition of severe pre-eclampsia. 59. However, severe pre-eclampsia is generally characterized by features such as severe hypertension (blood pressure of at least 160 mmHg systolic or 110 mmHg diastolic), severe proteinuria (at least 3 g of protein in 24 hours or 3+ on a dipstick), reduced urinary output (less than 400 to 500 mL in 24 hours), neurological disturbances (e.g., headache, visual disturbances, exaggerated tendon reflexes), upper abdominal pain, pulmonary edema (fluid in the lungs), and impaired liver function tests.
